summary:
SpaceXtinSafe turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into spacecraft-specific fire safety intelligence. It combines a knowledge-driven spacecraft digital twin, a Neo4j knowledge graph, machine learning and evidence-grounded AI. With it, users can investigate spacecraft materials, explore combustion behaviour within tested conditions, compare cabin environments and identify scientific uncertainties.

Every answer cites its NASA source. The Scientific Evidence Audit flags discrepancies between NASA datasets and published reports. The Virtual Fire Lab gives burning-rate estimates only where experimental data supports them, and declines otherwise. Research Gap Intelligence turns missing evidence and undocumented material interactions into proposed experiments. Simulated incident replays show how findings can inform research-based preparedness, without giving operational instructions.

In internal evaluation:

GraphRAG retrieved 2.48× more of the evidence needed for multi-step questions.
The prediction model cut error by 68%.
The live Copilot declined every question outside its evidence and gave no safety verdicts.
The deployed system passed all 23 end-to-end checks.

SpaceXtinSafe connects fragmented scientific research to practical spacecraft fire safety investigations. It helps researchers see what is known, what can be estimated and what still needs to be discovered.
details:
SpaceXtinSafe — From Research to Readiness

Fire behaves differently beyond Earth. Microgravity changes flame behaviour, oxygen transport and combustion dynamics, so fire-safety assumptions from Earth are not enough for spacecraft. NASA has carried out extensive combustion research, but its findings are spread across experimental datasets, technical reports and presentations.

SpaceXtinSafe is an AI-powered research platform for spacecraft fire safety. It turns NASA combustion research into spacecraft-specific scientific insights, experimentally supported predictions and opportunities for further investigation.

How It Works

SpaceXtinSafe combines three layers of scientific intelligence:

1. Evidence Intelligence: what do we know?
Users configure an interactive spacecraft digital twin, defining its compartments, materials and cabin atmosphere. Our scientific Copilot uses GraphRAG: it combines keyword search, semantic retrieval and knowledge-graph traversal in Neo4j to connect materials, experiments, conditions and findings. Every answer cites the NASA source and page, shows the original evidence and states its limitations. The Copilot must cite only evidence it retrieved, and every number it states must appear in that evidence.

2. Predictive Intelligence: what can we estimate?
The Virtual Fire Lab uses regression models trained on NASA FLEX experimental data to estimate droplet burning rates. Before predicting, the system checks that the requested conditions fall inside the tested experimental domain. It shows an empirical uncertainty band where the data supports one, and declines when it doesn’t.

3. Research Gap Intelligence: what should we investigate next?
SpaceXtinSafe identifies:

  • materials with no evidence in its library,
  • conditions that were never tested, and
  • material interactions that are not documented.

It turns these gaps into proposed experiments. For example, it finds no documented interaction between the polyester lining and polyurethane foam padding of a spacecraft sleeping bag, and proposes a combined-sample test at the cabin’s conditions. It also separates three kinds of unknown: a gap in this library, a condition outside a model’s tested range, and a possible gap in the wider literature.

Users can combine findings, predictions, uncertainties and research opportunities into a spacecraft-specific PDF evidence report. An 18-step guided tour walks first-time visitors through the full workflow.

Scientific Validity

SpaceXtinSafe integrates five NASA Physical Sciences Informatics datasets: FLEX (PSI-69), Saffire-I, II and III (PSI-98, 99, 100) and BASS-II (PSI-25). It also draws on 13 NASA publications, from which 42 findings were curated, each quote checked word for word against its source.

Our internal evaluations, run with frozen test sets, show:

  • 2.48× multi-hop retrieval recall: GraphRAG raised Recall@5 from 23.8% to 59.1% compared with hybrid retrieval alone.
  • 68.2% lower prediction error: the methanol burning-rate model reached an out-of-fold R² of 0.835 with leave-one-session-out validation. Its predictive skill is 0.68, with a 95% session-bootstrap interval of 0.54 to 0.78 and no systematic bias.
  • Live scientific Copilot:
    • 14 of 15 cases passed on the original test set.
    • 18 of 20 passed on a new set of questions written from the NASA papers and frozen before testing.
    • All 5 questions about facts outside the library were declined, and no answer gave a safety verdict.
  • Research gap benchmark: in 30 frozen cases, all 17 gaps were found with no false gaps, and missing evidence was never treated as evidence of safety.
  • Deployed system: all 23 end-to-end checks passed on the live site, including live Claude answers and Neo4j retrieval verified against the reference graph.

Our auditing system also finds discrepancies between datasets and published reports. For FLEX Test 70, the burning-rate constant is 0.41 mm²/s in the dataset and 0.56 mm²/s in the NASA report, so that test was excluded from model fitting.

These results show the prototype works in internal evaluation; they are not independent scientific validation.

Benefits and Intended Impact

SpaceXtinSafe aims to help combustion researchers, spacecraft engineers and mission planners:

  • find and synthesise relevant NASA evidence,
  • assess how existing research applies to a specific spacecraft,
  • explore combustion behaviour within experimentally supported limits,
  • identify conflicting measurements and missing evidence, and
  • plan future experiments and prioritise research.

In an automated comparison on five matched research tasks, SpaceXtinSafe reached every curated reference finding and stated where evidence was absent. Keyword search of the same NASA papers missed the reference pages in three of four tasks. A protocol for a timed user study is ready; we have not yet measured time savings.

Possible applications range from orbital research laboratories to lunar habitats and long-duration missions, where different gravity and cabin conditions raise new scientific questions.

Technology and Innovation

SpaceXtinSafe is built with React, Vite, Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, NumPy, SciPy, Neo4j AuraDB, NetworkX, Sentence Transformers and the Anthropic Claude API. It is deployed on Render and Vercel, with code on GitHub. Questions are routed by complexity: calculations and inventories are answered directly in Python, scientific questions go to Claude Sonnet, and complex synthesis goes to Claude Opus.

Our innovation lies in combining spacecraft digital twins, GraphRAG, constrained predictive modelling, evidence auditing and research gap identification in one connected research workflow.

Unlike typical AI applications, SpaceXtinSafe treats missing evidence, uncertainty and conflicting measurements as useful scientific outputs, not obstacles to producing an answer.

Responsible Design

Team Spaceon prioritised scientific accuracy, transparency, experimental applicability, computational efficiency and responsible AI. The platform preserves evidence provenance, avoids unsupported extrapolation and separates observed findings from model estimates. It never gives safety verdicts, fire-risk scores or emergency instructions.

SpaceXtinSafe is an independent research prototype. It is not a certified fire-safety simulator, an operational emergency system or a NASA-endorsed product.

Live app: https://space-xtin-safe.vercel.app
Source code: https://github.com/lucwu00/SpaceXtinSafe

We do not simply predict how fire behaves in space. We help researchers understand what we know, what we do not know, and what we need to investigate next.
